client: I've been really struggling at work since my grandma passed away last month. I keep zoning out during meetings because I'll suddenly remember little things about her, like how she used to make my favorite cookies whenever I visited. It's making me anxious because I'm falling behind on projects, but when I try to focus, I just start thinking about how I'll never get to hear her voice again.
therapist: I hear how deeply you're grieving your grandma's passing, and it makes complete sense that these precious memories would come up during your workday. It sounds like you're carrying both the sadness of loss and anxiety about falling behind - that's a lot to hold at once. What would it feel like to acknowledge that these moments of remembering her are actually expressions of your love for her?

client:
I guess I never thought about it that way - that missing her at work could be because I love her so much. But it still feels like a distraction I can't afford. When I start crying at my desk, I panic about looking unprofessional or getting fired. 

The idea of it being love makes me feel a little softer, but also more guilty - like if I accept these moments, am I just giving myself permission to fall apart?
therapist: It's beautiful that you're able to connect these painful moments to love, and I understand your worry about balancing grief with professional responsibilities. That guilt you're feeling might be coming from judging your very human response to loss - what would it look like to treat yourself with the same compassion your grandma showed you?

client: I hear what you're saying about self-compassion, but it's hard to imagine treating myself the way my grandma treated me. She was so patient and understanding, and I just don't feel like I deserve that same kindness right now. Every time I try to be gentle with myself, I just end up feeling even more guilty for not being more productive or pulled together at work.
therapist: It sounds like you're holding yourself to much higher standards than your grandma ever would, and that disconnect between how she saw you and how you're seeing yourself is causing extra pain. What might change if you considered that honoring your grief could actually be the most productive thing you could do for yourself right now?

client:
I know she wouldn't want me to be this hard on myself, but I can't help feeling like I should be handling this better. When you say "honoring my grief," it sounds nice in theory, but I worry if I let myself really feel it, I'll just fall apart completely. 

The productive thing would be getting back to normal, wouldn't it? That's what everyone seems to expect from me anyway.
therapist: Your grandma's passing is still so recent, and the pressure to "get back to normal" might be making this grief feel even heavier to carry. What if "handling it better" actually means allowing yourself to feel this loss fully, rather than pushing through it?

client:
I know you're right about needing to feel the grief, but it's just so overwhelming. Every time I start to really let it in, I panic because it feels like I'll never stop crying. And then I feel guilty for falling apart when my family seems to be handling it better than me. 

Part of me worries that if I actually let myself feel this fully, I'll become that sad person everyone avoids. My grandma wouldn't have wanted me to be like this.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying not just the grief itself, but also fear about what might happen if you truly let yourself experience it - that's an incredibly heavy burden. What if the tears aren't a sign you're falling apart, but rather your heart's way of honoring how much she meant to you?

client: I guess I never thought of it that way before. But what if the tears don't stop once I start? I'm scared I'll just drown in them and never be able to function again. My mom always said I needed to be strong, and breaking down feels like I'm failing her.
therapist: It sounds like you've been carrying this belief that being strong means not showing your pain, and that letting yourself grieve would mean failing both your mom and your grandma. But real strength often looks like allowing ourselves to feel our emotions fully - what might it feel like to gently challenge that idea that tears mean weakness?

client: I get what you're saying, but it still feels so complicated. My mom always told me I had to be strong for grandma, especially after grandpa passed. If I start letting myself feel everything now, it’s like I’m betraying that promise I made to them both. What if I just fall apart and can’t stop? Weakness feels dangerous, like it could swallow me whole.
therapist: It makes so much sense that this feels complicated when you've carried this responsibility of being strong for your family for so long. That fear of being swallowed by grief is very real, but I wonder what it would be like to consider that maybe the strength you've shown all these years is exactly what will help you navigate these waves of emotion when they come?

client:
I don't know... I've always been the one holding everything together. If I start letting myself feel all this grief, what if I just fall apart completely? That's what scares me the most. My family depends on me being strong. 

It's hard to imagine that the same strength could help me through falling apart when I've spent my whole life making sure I don't.
therapist: You've been the rock for your family for so long that it's understandable this idea of letting go feels terrifying - like the whole structure might collapse. But what if true strength includes knowing when to lean into the support you've so generously given others?

client:
I get what you're saying, but it's not that simple. Every time I've tried to lean on others before, they either let me down or made me feel like a burden. The thought of everything falling apart because I'm not holding it together is just... paralyzing. 

I know logically that people should support each other, but in my experience, if I don't do everything myself, it won't get done right. That's why this "leaning on others" idea makes me so anxious.
therapist: It sounds like past experiences have taught you that relying on others leads to disappointment, which makes this idea of vulnerability feel especially risky right now. That deep fear of things falling apart if you're not in control is completely understandable given what you've been through - what would it look like to start with just one small way of reaching out that feels safe to you?

client:
I get what you're saying about starting small, but even that feels terrifying. What if I try reaching out to someone and they don't respond the way I hope? I've been let down so many times before that it's hard to imagine a different outcome now. 

The idea of being vulnerable makes my chest feel tight - like I'm setting myself up for more pain. Maybe it's easier to just keep handling everything myself, even if it's lonely.
therapist: I hear how deeply protective that instinct to handle everything yourself has been, and how painful those past letdowns were. That tightness in your chest tells me how scary it feels to imagine risking vulnerability again - what if we explore what a truly safe, small first step might look like, one where the risk of disappointment feels manageable?
